title: Tools
text:
This page collects resources I’ve found useful in my own research, most of which centres on Discrete Choice Experiments and Q-methodology. Materials here are organised around these two methods.


A few resources that make it easier to get started with a Q-study:

To collect data online, Aproxima offers a neat, free tool for running a Q-sort.
For analysis, Aiora Zabala’s R package qmethod covers the full workflow from data import to factor rotation.
If you’re not familiar with R, the same author also provides a Shiny app version of qmethod with a graphical interface.
To understand what the code is actually doing, I recommend the qmethod Cookbook, or a little more humbly an annotated example file I put together myself.

title: Christoph Schulze
text:
I am a Postdoc researcher in the Governance of Ecosystem Services working group at the Leibniz Centre for Agricultural Landscape Research (ZALF).
My research asks how innovative governance mechanisms can support the transition to sustainable food systems. I work on collective and result-based agri-environmental contracts, on eco-labels, and on voluntary markets for biodiversity, studying how farmers, food companies, and consumers respond to them. To do this I combine Discrete Choice Experiments, behavioural games, and Q-methodology.
I am especially interested in questions of institutional design. Who contracts with whom? How are outcomes rewarded? How long do agreements run? These details often matter more for uptake than the payment level does, and they are easy to overlook when schemes are designed from the top down.

title: CBEAR meets REECAP
text:
It all started in June 2022, when I met Tongzhe Li at the REECAP meeting in Uppsala, Sweden. Tongzhe, an active member of the CBEAR network in North America, had come across the pond to tell us about the FARE Lab she had just established at the University of Guelph. I was lucky enough to grab one of her FARE Lab t-shirts, which has reminded me of her lab in Canada ever since.
Now, in 2026, I finally took the opportunity to visit her and present potential research ideas that could be implemented at the Innovation Centre for Agricultural System Transformation (IAT) at ZALF, such as auction designs for agri-environmental contracts, for example. I gave a talk on Farmer Behavior in Agri-Environmental Contract Design.
I’m very glad about how things worked out, and I’m looking forward to seeing how future projects in Germany can draw on the experiences gained from auction research in Canada.

title: New paper in Q Open
text:
Together with Julian Sagebiel and Jens Rommel, we published a paper entitled “A Pre-Registration Template for Transparent Choice Experiment Research” in Q Open, advocating for the use of pre-registration templates for choice experiments. The article can be found here.
This article grew out of a simple frustration that generic pre-registration templates (like the ones from the Open Science Framework) work fine for a randomized controlled trial, but they don’t really ask the questions that matter for a discrete choice experiment. Things like how you selected your bid vector or priors for an efficient design, whether you’re using a random utility or random regret model, or how you plan to handle preference heterogeneity and protest responses.
So we built a template that does. It’s organized into four parts: general information (hypotheses, sample, exclusion criteria), experimental design (choice scenario, statistical design, priors), estimation (welfare measures, heterogeneity, handling of outliers), and validity (follow-up questions, budget reminders, and the like). The idea isn’t to force researchers to commit to a specific model before they’ve even seen the data. That would be unrealistic, since things like distributional assumptions for random parameters often can’t be decided from theory alone. Instead, the template asks researchers to document their decision rules in advance, so it’s transparent which choices were fixed before data collection and which were made afterward.
We think this kind of transparency matters especially for our field, where welfare estimates often feed directly into policy decisions, and where critics have long argued that choice experiments can be (deliberately or not) designed or analyzed in ways that push results in a particular direction.
The template is open source and available on Zenodo in several formats (PDF, DOCX, HTML, LaTeX, and Quarto), and the source code lives on GitHub, where we’re hoping others in the community will help us improve it over time.

title: New paper in JEEM
text:
Our paper “Convergent Validity in Incentive-Compatible Contingent Valuation: Bid-vector and elicitation format effects” is now published in the Special Issue on Non-Market Valuation in the Journal of Environmental Economics and Management (JEEM). It was quite a long road, starting with a discussion of which elicitation format we should use in our study. Every co-author had a different opinion, and in the end we couldn’t settle on just one. The only way forward was to apply all of them in a pre-registered experimental design and see whether they converged. This process really shows how great research papers are often the product of curiosity, rather than a strict response to an advertised research call. I’m really glad about how it worked out in the end.
The paper essentially tests whether three “theory-driven” ways of asking people about their willingness to pay, a simple yes/no vote, a payment card, and an open-ended question, actually agree with each other once you try to make them all incentive-compatible. We ran a large pre-registered survey (over 12,000 people across six European countries) asking about willingness to pay for an EU-wide biodiversity program, and we also varied the range of amounts people were shown. We find that the formats don’t agree: people’s stated willingness to pay differs substantially depending on which format they got, and even within the same format, it changes depending on which range of amounts was shown. Some of this comes down to behavioral factors (people tend to just keep saying “yes” as the amounts get higher in the simple yes/no format), but some of it also comes down to how the underlying statistics are modeled, which was a bit of a surprising twist for us.
The paper can be found here.

text:
Visionary



Food systems

Discrete Choice Experiments

Q-methodology

Factorial Survey Experiments



Visionary (Horizon Europe, 2022-2026) studied behavioural drivers of the transition to sustainable food systems. I led the work package task investigating whether a governmental biodiversity label increases farmers’ willingness to adopt targeted conservation measures, via a Discrete Choice Experiment across four countries.












Contracts2.0



Discrete Choice Experiments

Public Goods Games



Contracts2.0 (Horizon 2020, 2019-2023) co-designed novel contract models for agri-environmental measures, combining results-based, collective, land tenure and value chain approaches across eleven innovation labs in nine European countries. I worked in the work package on ex-ante analysis of novel contracts, leading the task on consumer preferences for label-based approaches that bundle ecosystem service provision with agricultural products, studied through Discrete Choice Experiments in several European countries.












AgoraNatura



Discrete Choice Experiments



AgoraNatura (BMBF, 2016–2020) developed a web-based marketplace matching landowners offering privately financed conservation measures with buyers willing to pay for them. I worked in the sub-project on institutional analysis, studying farmers’ ex ante preferences for such contracts via a Discrete Choice Experiment.

title: Teaching

I teach environmental and agricultural economics at bachelor’s and master’s level, with a focus on how economic tools are used in environmental policy and on the methods of non-market valuation. At PhD level, I teach methods courses covering Discrete Choice Experiments and Q-methodology.

A methods course in the research school People, Society and Sustainability, covering random utility theory, econometric models for discrete dependent variables, principles of experimental design, and the estimation of choice models in R using Apollo.

Co-lecturer, since 2020
A one week hands-on training course covering economic experiments, Q-methodology, social network analysis.



As part of projects in the Governance of Ecosystem Services working group, I have supervised one bachelor’s and three master’s theses on agri-environmental policy, environmental valuation, and behavioural approaches to farmer decision-making.
